prompt: In a C–Mg bond (magnesium, EN 1.31; carbon, EN 2.55), which atom carries the δ−?
choices: Carbon — it is the MORE electronegative of the two
explanation: Carbon at 2.55 is well above magnesium at 1.31, so carbon pulls the electron density and ends up partially negative.
teach: Almost every bond you meet has carbon as the δ+ partner. Bonds to metals are the exception — and that reversal is the entire point of organometallic reagents.

prompt: A carbon bearing δ− behaves as:
choices: A nucleophile — it is electron-rich and will attack electron-poor centres
explanation: Electron-rich means nucleophilic. A carbon made δ− by a metal will attack δ+ carbons, such as those in carbonyls.
teach: This is why Grignard and organolithium reagents matter: they invert carbon's usual role, letting you form new carbon-carbon bonds.

prompt: Which of these bonds puts the partial NEGATIVE charge on carbon?
explanation: Lithium (0.98) is far below carbon (2.55), so carbon takes the electron density. In C–O, C–Cl and C–N, the other atom is more electronegative and carbon is δ+.
teach: Run the electronegativity comparison every time. Metals sit far below carbon; O, N and the halogens sit above it.

prompt: In the B–H bonds of sodium borohydride (boron 2.04, hydrogen 2.20), which atom is δ−?
choices: Hydrogen — it is slightly more electronegative than boron
explanation: Hydrogen edges out boron, so these hydrogens carry partial negative charge — they are hydride-like and can be delivered to an electron-poor carbon.
teach: This is why NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are reducing agents: their hydrogens are δ− and behave as hydride donors, unlike the δ+ hydrogen of an acid.

prompt: In the Al–H bonds of LiAlH₄ (aluminium 1.61, hydrogen 2.20), the hydrogens are:
choices: δ− and strongly hydride-donating — a larger gap than in B–H, so a stronger reducing agent
explanation: The Al–H gap (0.59) is much larger than the B–H gap (0.16), so LiAlH₄'s hydrogens are far more hydride-like — which is exactly why it is the stronger and less selective reducer.
teach: The relative strength of these two reagents follows straight from electronegativity differences, rather than being a fact to memorize.

prompt: Which statement about hydrogen's partial charge is correct?
choices: H is δ+ when bonded to O, N or a halogen, but δ− when bonded to a metal like Al or B
H is never part of a polar bond
explanation: Hydrogen sits in the middle of the electronegativity range, so its partial charge depends entirely on its partner: below O and N it is δ+, above Al and B it is δ−.
teach: Acidic H (δ+, on O/N) versus hydride H (δ−, on a metal) is the same atom playing opposite roles. Always compare it against its partner.

prompt: Which metals are LESS electronegative than carbon, and therefore leave carbon δ− when bonded to it?
choices: Li, Na, K, Mg and Al — all of them
None; all metals are more electronegative than carbon
explanation: Li 0.98, Na 0.93, K 0.82, Mg 1.31, Al 1.61 — every one sits well below carbon's 2.55.
teach: Metals occupy the bottom-left of the periodic table, where electronegativity is lowest. Any carbon-metal bond therefore polarizes toward carbon.

prompt: Why is a carbanion (carbon with a lone pair and a negative charge) an extremely strong base?
choices: Carbon holds negative charge poorly, since it is not very electronegative — so the anion is unstable and reactive
Carbon is highly electronegative and stabilizes the charge well
Carbon cannot carry a negative charge
explanation: Negative charge is only comfortable on electronegative atoms. Carbon is mediocre at it, so a carbanion is desperate to donate that pair — hence methane's pKa of about 50.
teach: The same rule that ranks acid strength runs backwards here: the worse an atom holds negative charge, the stronger a base its anion is.
